basics.name: Adhesive reference works and classifications: Edward M. Petrie's 'Handbook of Adhesives and Sealants' (McGraw Hill), the Adhesive and Sealant Council's adhesives.org portal plus the ASC-CATIA-FEICA 'Adhesives & Sealants Classification Manual', and Wikipedia's 'Adhesive' and 'List of glues' articles
basics.url: Three main pages, all opened. (1) ASC adhesive technologies page: https://adhesives.org/adhesives-sealants/adhesives-sealants-overview/adhesive-technologies/ (2) Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adhesive and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_glues (3) Petrie, publisher page for the 3rd edition: https://www.mheducation.com/highered/mhp/product/handbook-adhesives-sealants-third-edition.html . Also opened: the free classification manual PDF https://adhesives.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/ASC-CATIA-FEICA-Adhesives-and-Sealants-Classification-Manual-2021.pdf , the ASC consumer/DIY page https://adhesives.org/markets/consumer-do-it-yourself/ , and Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Adhesives
basics.resource_type: Mixed: book (Petrie's handbook), classification system (ASC-CATIA-FEICA manual), industry portal (adhesives.org, run by a trade association) and encyclopedia/wiki (Wikipedia)
basics.cost: Wikipedia, adhesives.org and the classification manual PDF are free. Petrie 3rd edition: eBook from 114 USD and print from 126 USD on the McGraw Hill page (checked September 2026). Amazon lists the hardcover at 132.98 USD and Apple Books lists the eBook at 99.99 USD. It is also part of McGraw Hill's AccessEngineering online library, which is sold as an institutional subscription; that page returned 403 to us, so access terms there are not verified [uncertain]
basics.license: Petrie: all rights reserved (commercial book), so link to it and cite it, but don't copy text, tables or figures. adhesives.org: '© Adhesives.org' footer with no open licence, so treat it as all rights reserved: link, and paraphrase with a citation. The classification manual PDF shows no licence statement; it is free to download, and its category names and numbers can be cited as facts. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA 4.0 (licence link on the page), so it can be adapted with attribution and share-alike
basics.language: English for all three. The Wikipedia 'Adhesive' article has many language versions (e.g. German 'Klebstoff', Spanish 'Adhesivo', Czech 'Lepidlo'), which is useful for translations. FEICA's first (1996) European manual was printed in three languages, according to the 2021 manual's introduction
basics.year: Petrie: 1st edition 1999/2000 (ISBN 0070498881; Google Books gives 880 or 896 pages); 2nd edition 2 January 2007 (ISBN 9780071479165; about 800 print pages per Amazon, 1048 per Google Books); 3rd edition published 9 December 2020, copyright 2021 (ISBN 9781260440447; 784 pages per Amazon and Apple; Open Library says 560 pages, so the page count is disputed [uncertain]). ASC founded 1958; the adhesive technologies page was last modified 21 September 2023; the portal posts news up to September 2026. Classification manual: FEICA's European manual 1996; sealants added 2008; joint ASC-CATIA-FEICA manual 2012; current 2021 edition (PDF dated February 2021). Wikipedia 'Adhesive' last edited 28 August 2026; 'List of glues' last edited 7 December 2024
basics.access_barrier: Wikipedia, adhesives.org and the manual: none. Petrie: paywall (buy it, borrow from a library, or use an institutional AccessEngineering licence)
basics.image_license: Wikipedia's images are on Wikimedia Commons, each with its own free licence (e.g. the glue-gun photo, the adhesive fracture diagram 'AdhesiveFractures.svg' and 'Fracture_modes_v2.svg'); check each file page before reuse. adhesives.org images and videos: all rights reserved, or third-party YouTube videos [uncertain]. The manual PDF is text only. Petrie's figures and tables: all rights reserved (Google Books describes the book as 'illustrated')
basics.authority_level: Petrie: professional reference by an expert author (about 50 years in the adhesives industry, formerly at Westinghouse and ABB, technical adviser to SpecialChem), from a major engineering publisher. ASC: the US industry trade association (founded 1958; 110 member companies, 'more than 75% of the U.S. industry'), so manufacturer-backed. Classification manual: the joint industry classification of ASC (North America), FEICA (Europe) and CATIA (China), which together cover more than 70% of the world market. Wikipedia: community or unvetted, with citations

coverage.covers: Only adhesives and sealants (bonding), not mechanical connections. PETRIE (2nd edition chapter list from the back cover): Introduction to Adhesives and Sealants; Theories of Adhesion; Properties of Adhesive Materials and the Interphase Region; Surfaces and Surface Preparation; Joint Design; Test Methods; Classification and Formulation; Thermosetting Types; Elastomeric Types; Thermoplastic Types; Naturally Occurring Types; Specialty Adhesives; Selection of Adhesives and Sealants; Bonding and Sealing Specific Substrates; Effect of the Environment; Application Processes; Environmental and Safety Factors; Adhesive Use in Various Industries (18 chapters). The 3rd edition adds sustainability (biopolymers, biodegradable adhesives, fewer solvent fumes (VOCs)), removable adhesives, nanotechnology and 'multi-tasking materials'. It covers bonding metals, plastics, composites and elastomers. The full 3rd-edition chapter list was not visible (AccessEngineering blocked) [uncertain]. ASC PORTAL: 'Adhesive Technologies' explains four 'physically hardening' families (hot melt; organic solvent-based, split into wet-bonding and contact adhesives; plastisol; water-based, split into solutions and dispersions) with typical uses. A consumer/DIY page describes 'four main types of consumer glues' and what each suits: multipurpose (polyurethane, with contact cement as an alternative) for ceramics, plastics, wood and some metals; instant/super (cyanoacrylate) for plastic, wood and ceramics; wood glue; and quick-set two-part epoxy for wood, ceramics and other rigid materials. There are also pages on adhesion science, joint design, surface treatment, and adhesives versus mechanical fasteners. CLASSIFICATION MANUAL (18 pages): definitions of adhesive, sealant and pressure-sensitive adhesive (sticky tape adhesive); 4 kinds of pressure-sensitive tape (single coated, double coated, reinforced, unsupported/transfer); 7 adhesive market segments; 7 adhesive product categories with about 45 chemistry subcategories; 4 sealant market segments; 9 sealant product categories. WIKIPEDIA: 'Adhesive' covers history, types by reactiveness and by origin, application, how adhesion works, improving adhesion, electrically debondable adhesives, health, failure (cohesive, adhesive and mixed fracture) and joint design. 'List of glues' tabulates about 50 glue types in 4 groups (plant- and animal-based; solvent-type; synthetic monomer; synthetic polymer, split into thermoplastic and thermosetting). Category:Adhesives holds about 98 articles and 3 subcategories (Adhesive tape, Microscopy mountants, Woodworking adhesives)
coverage.organisation: Petrie: by topic, from theory to joint design, testing, adhesive families (by polymer type), selection, substrates and applications. It's a handbook read by chapter and works if you already know the family names. ASC: website menu (Adhesives 101 → overview → technologies; science of adhesion; fastening and bonding; markets). Families are grouped by how they harden, which suits beginners, but only the physically hardening group is written up on the technologies page. Manual: numbered codes (e.g. 2.5.4 Acrylates, including cyanoacrylate and anaerobics), grouped partly by chemistry and partly by physical form (dispersion, hot melt, solvent, reactive, water-soluble). It's built for market statistics, so it's hard for beginners. Wikipedia: nested headings (By reactiveness → Non-reactive: drying, pressure-sensitive, contact, hot; Reactive: anaerobic, multi-part, pre-mixed and frozen, one-part), then By origin (natural / synthetic). The question 'how does it harden?' is easy to follow without knowing chemistry names
coverage.scope_match: medium: adhesive TYPES are in scope, and these are the authoritative sources for the family names and how each family hardens. But they are industrial and general, with nothing specific on 3D-printing plastics (PLA, PETG, resin) and no mechanisms. They are best used as the naming and classification backbone for the adhesive branch, with maker test data from other sources
coverage.taxonomy_used: Four overlapping schemes. (1) By how it hardens (Wikipedia; ASC): non-reactive or 'physically hardening' (it dries as water or solvent evaporates, cools as with hot melt, or stays permanently tacky as with pressure-sensitive adhesives) versus reactive or 'chemically curing' (two-part mix; one-part cured by moisture, heat, UV light or no air (anaerobic)). Wikipedia has 2 top groups with 4 + 4 subtypes; ASC lists 4 physically hardening families. (2) By chemistry and form (ASC-CATIA-FEICA manual): 7 top-level product groups: 2.1 natural polymers (starch/dextrin, protein such as casein and soy, animal glue); 2.2 polymer dispersion/emulsion (PVAc, EVA, acrylic, SBR, other latex including polychloroprene, natural rubber latex, polyurethane dispersion); 2.3 hot melt (polyolefin, EVA, polyamide, polyester, styrene block copolymers, polyurethane including moisture-cure, acrylic); 2.4 solvent-based (polychloroprene, polyurethane, rubbers, acrylic, silicone, PVC copolymers); 2.5 reactive (epoxy; polyurethane; unsaturated polyester; acrylates including cyanoacrylate, anaerobic/dimethacrylate and second-generation structural acrylics; silicone; formaldehyde condensates such as phenolic, urea, melamine and resorcinol; silane-modified polymers); 2.6 water-soluble polymers (polyvinyl alcohol, cellulose ethers, methylcellulose, CMC, PVP); 2.7 other. (3) By origin: natural versus synthetic (Wikipedia; the manual's 2.1). (4) Petrie: by polymer behaviour (thermosetting, elastomeric, thermoplastic, naturally occurring, specialty), which gives 5 type chapters
coverage.example_types: cyanoacrylate / superglue (moisture-curing one-part); two-part epoxy (multi-part reactive); polyvinyl acetate (PVAc) white glue and yellow 'aliphatic resin' wood glue (polymer dispersion, drying); contact adhesive / contact cement (polychloroprene or natural rubber, coat both sides then press); solvent cement / solvent welding (acetone for ABS, MEK for polystyrene, dichloromethane for polycarbonate and acrylic/PMMA); hot-melt adhesive (EVA glue-gun sticks; also reactive polyurethane hot melts); pressure-sensitive adhesive (tapes, labels, removable and repositionable adhesives); anaerobic adhesive (thread-locking fluid); UV / light-curing adhesive (usually acrylic); heat-curing one-part epoxy; moisture-curing polyurethane (foaming 'multipurpose' glue); second-generation structural acrylic (SGA / methacrylate); silicone adhesive and sealant; silane-modified polymer (MS polymer) adhesive/sealant; construction adhesive; plastisol (PVC paste cured by heat); animal / hide glue (reversible with heat and water); casein and starch/dextrin glues; resorcinol- and urea-formaldehyde glues (exterior wood, plywood); electrically debondable adhesive (releases when a current is applied); pre-mixed and frozen (PMF) adhesives
coverage.making_methods: General engineering and manufacturing (automotive, aerospace, construction, packaging, electronics, footwear, woodworking and joinery). There is a little on consumer/DIY use (ASC consumer page; the manual's segment 1.4.1). Nothing is aimed at 3D printing
coverage.item_count: Manual: 7 adhesive product categories with about 45 chemistry subcategories, plus 9 sealant categories. Wikipedia 'Adhesive': 2 reactiveness groups with 8 named subtypes, plus 2 origin groups. 'List of glues': about 50 glue types in 4 tables. Category:Adhesives: about 98 articles. Petrie 2nd edition: 18 chapters (about 800 to 1,048 pages)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Adhesive types: yes, this is the core. Chemistries covered: cyanoacrylate, epoxy, PVAc, contact, solvent, hot melt, pressure-sensitive, anaerobic, UV, polyurethane, silicone, MS polymer, animal/natural. Material and use advice: ASC's consumer page (CA for plastic, wood and ceramics, needs a tight fit and fills no gaps; epoxy for wood, ceramics and rigid materials, fills gaps, water resistant, undo only 'with a hammer and chisel'; polyurethane for ceramics, plastics, wood and some metals, foams and needs clamping; wood glue for wood, clamp, 24 to 72 hours). ASC notes that water-based glues need at least one porous surface (wood, paper, fabric, leather) and that hot melts suit porous materials but creep under load. Wikipedia and the List of glues give solvents per plastic (acetone for ABS, MEK for polystyrene, dichloromethane for polycarbonate and PMMA) and warn that low-surface-energy plastics bond poorly without surface treatment (plasma, flame, primer). Petrie has a 'Bonding and Sealing Specific Substrates' chapter covering plastics, but whether it covers 3D-printing plastics like PLA or PETG is not known [uncertain]. Hand-release and reversible bonds: hot melts can be heated to undo and re-attach (ASC); removable and repositionable pressure-sensitive adhesives (Wikipedia; the manual); electrically debondable adhesives (Wikipedia); hide glue reversibility; 'removable adhesives' added in Petrie's 3rd edition. Self-locking: anaerobic thread-lockers stop screws loosening (Wikipedia; the manual). Not covered: torque-limiting, one-way/ratchet, indexing, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors
coverage.entry_structure: Wikipedia: each type has a short plain paragraph with examples and typical uses, some with a photo, and links to a main article (e.g. Hot-melt adhesive, Pressure-sensitive adhesive). The 'List of glues' tables have columns for type, subtypes, sources, manufacture, chemistry, fumes (volatiles), safety, properties, shelf life, working time, setting, strength, solvents, uses and date, but many cells are empty. ASC: an essay-style paragraph per family (how it works, pros and cons, industrial uses, forms supplied, e.g. hot-melt sticks for glue guns). Manual: a numbered code, a name and a short note of what's included and excluded. Petrie: long chapters with formulations, property tables, test methods and design guidance (from the publisher and Google Books descriptions)
coverage.audience_level: Petrie: professional (end users, formulators, marketers, design engineers), written so that 'those new to the field' get a fundamental knowledge base. ASC: designers and industry, plus one consumer/DIY page. Manual: industry and market analysts. Wikipedia: general public or undergraduate

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium overall. Wikipedia 'Adhesive' is high: plain wording, the reactive/non-reactive split and everyday examples (glue gun, Post-it notes, superglue). The ASC consumer page is high, with four household glue types and what they stick. ASC's technologies page is medium: clear, but written for industry. The manual is low: a market-code list with chemical names. Petrie is low to medium: thorough, but long, technical and paywalled
usefulness.has_images: Wikipedia 'Adhesive': yes, about a dozen photos and diagrams (e.g. glue gun, casein glue, fracture-mode diagrams); 'List of glues' has 1 to 2 photos. adhesives.org: mostly text with some stock photos and video thumbnails [uncertain]. Manual: no images. Petrie: illustrated, with many tables and figures (per Google Books and the descriptions)
usefulness.has_animations: adhesives.org has a videos section and embeds a James May video explaining how glue works on its homepage. Wikipedia and Petrie: no
usefulness.gaps: Nothing on 3D-printing plastics (PLA, PETG, ASA, resin) or which glue suits which printed material. No simple 'this material to that material' matrix; Wikipedia only links out to the thistothat.com glue selector. The ASC technologies page describes only the physically hardening families; reactive types (CA, epoxy, anaerobic, UV) are covered only on the DIY page and in the manual. The manual is market segmentation, not selection help. 'List of glues' has been flagged incomplete since August 2008, with many empty cells. Few beginner numbers (strengths, gap sizes, cure times) except the DIY page's cure times. Petrie is paywalled and pitched at industry. None explains solvent welding of printed parts, surface prep for low-energy plastics in beginner terms, or glue-plus-mechanical hybrid joints
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Yes for Wikipedia, which has stable per-type articles, e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adhesive (overview; section anchors such as #Contact and #Hot); related articles titled Cyanoacrylate, Hot-melt adhesive, Pressure-sensitive adhesive, Polyvinyl acetate, Epoxy, Solvent bonding, Thread-locking compound and Construction adhesive appear in Category:Adhesives. ASC: one long page for all technologies (no per-type URLs), but good as a 'how glues harden' citation. The manual PDF has a stable URL and is good for citing the official category code of each family. Petrie: cite by chapter; there are no free per-chapter pages
usefulness.reusable_data: Wikipedia: yes. It's CC BY-SA 4.0, and the category tree and articles are available through the MediaWiki API; the 'List of glues' tables can be scraped (with attribution and share-alike). Manual: not a dataset, but the numbered list is short enough to rebuild by hand, and names and codes are citable facts (no licence stated). ASC and Petrie text: not reusable, so link and paraphrase
usefulness.maintained: Wikipedia 'Adhesive' is actively edited (28 August 2026). adhesives.org is live with news posted September 2026, though its technologies page was last modified in September 2023. The manual's current edition is 2021 (updated about every 9 years: 2012, then 2021). Petrie's 3rd edition (December 2020) is still sold in 2026
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Use 'How does it harden?' as the first adhesive question, in plain words with the term in brackets: dries (evaporative / drying), cools (hot melt), stays sticky (pressure-sensitive), or reacts: two-part mix (multi-part reactive), air moisture (moisture-cure, e.g. CA), no air plus metal (anaerobic), UV light (light-cure), heat (heat-cure). (2) ASC's wet-bond versus contact-bond method (coat both sides, let it dry, then press) as a 'how you apply it' tag. (3) ASC's selection triad as flow-chart questions: What are you bonding (same or different, porous or smooth)? How will you apply it? How will it be used (strength, heat, water)? (4) A 'can it be undone?' filter: hot melt reheats, CA dissolves with debonder or acetone, hide glue with heat and water, PSA peels, epoxy and solvent welds are permanent. (5) Wikipedia's failure types (adhesive failure versus cohesive failure versus the part breaking) to explain test results. (6) The manual's numeric codes as a cross-reference column so each entry can cite its official family. (7) Link to the 'porous substrate needed' rule for water-based glues
usefulness.design_rules_given: Some general numbers: hot melts are applied at 65 to 180 °C (Wikipedia); plastisols cure at 150 to 180 °C (ASC); PMF adhesives are stored at or below −40 °C; UV adhesives cure in as little as 1 second; consumer cure times are about 24 hours for polyurethane and epoxy, from 16 hours for contact cement, and 24 to 72 hours for wood glue (ASC DIY page). Joint design: large bonded area, loaded mainly in shear (sliding, mode II) rather than peel or tension (Wikipedia). Petrie has full chapters on joint design, stress and test methods, but the specific numbers were not viewed [uncertain]
usefulness.file_formats: HTML (Wikipedia, adhesives.org); PDF (classification manual, 18 pages); print and eBook for Petrie (Adobe Digital Editions eBook from McGraw Hill; online chapters on AccessEngineering)
usefulness.terminology_value: High. Proper names and aliases: glue = adhesive = cement = mucilage = paste (the manual; Wikipedia); superglue / instant glue = cyanoacrylate; white glue = PVAc; yellow carpenter's glue = aliphatic resin (a PVAc variant); contact cement = contact adhesive (also 'impact glue'); hot glue = hot-melt adhesive; threadlocker = anaerobic adhesive; tape adhesive = pressure-sensitive adhesive (PSA); MS polymer = silane-modified polymer; SGA = second-generation (structural) acrylic; 'physically hardening' versus 'chemically curing'; wet bonding versus contact bonding; adherend or substrate (the part being glued); cohesive versus adhesive failure. Interlanguage links give translations
usefulness.decision_support: Limited. ASC's 'Adhesive Selection' page lists three questions (substrates; application restrictions; use requirements) with no logic behind them. ASC's 'Bonding Questionnaire' and 'Buyer's Marketplace' pass your requirements to supplier members or filter suppliers by market, technology and raw material, so they are sourcing tools, not selectors. The ASC DIY page is effectively a 4-row comparison of household glue types by material, gap filling, water resistance and cure time. Wikipedia has no selector, but links to thistothat.com (an 11-by-11 'this material to that material' glue picker). Petrie has a 'Selection of Adhesives and Sealants' chapter with selection tables (contents not viewed) [uncertain]
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Wikipedia's 'Adhesive' bibliography cites Ebnesajjad's Handbook of Adhesives and Surface Preparation, Kinloch's Adhesion and Adhesives, and Mittal and Pizzi's Handbook of Adhesive Technology (not Petrie). Its external links point to adhesives.org (as the 'Educational portal on adhesives and sealants'), RoyMech's adhesive bonding page and thistothat.com. The manual is the shared scheme behind ASC (US), FEICA (EU) and CATIA (China) market reports (ChemQuest and Smithers). Overlaps: DIN 8593-8 (adhesive bonding as a joining process, already in this project's prior-art list); RoyMech; the maker glue guides item (Prusa, CNC Kitchen), which supplies the 3D-printing material data these sources lack. Petrie also runs adhesive articles on SpecialChem (per his author bio). The ASC technologies text reads like an adaptation of a European (German) industry primer, but its source is not stated [uncertain]
